programmes.name: PM GatiShakti National Master Plan
programmes.lead_ministry: Ministry of Commerce & Industry (DPIIT, Logistics Division)
programmes.angle: India’s infrastructure coordination layer — and what it changes for industrial connectivity.
programmes.question: Which industrial nodes get their road, rail, port and logistics links planned together, and which still get them in sequence?
programmes.stage_note: The platform and its institutions are operating. It does not build infrastructure itself: it plans and evaluates projects that other programmes fund and build.

launch.label: Launched 13 Oct 2021; institutional framework cleared by the Cabinet on 21 Oct 2021

time_horizon.text: Standing institution with no end date. The 2021 plan set sectoral targets to 2024-25.

programmes.geography: National — central ministries and all 36 States/UTs on one geospatial platform

glance.label: Institutions
glance.value: Empowered Group of Secretaries (chaired by the Cabinet Secretary) · Network Planning Group · Technical Support Unit

glance.label: On the platform
glance.value: 57 central ministries/departments and 36 States/UTs; 1,700+ data layers

glance.label: Routing rule
glance.value: Logistics and connectivity projects above ₹500 crore go through the NPG

ledger.label: Institutional framework
ledger.value: EGoS, NPG and TSU approved by the Cabinet

ledger.label: Projects evaluated → sanctioned
ledger.value: 208 projects / ₹15.39 lakh crore assessed (Oct 2024) → 396 / ₹18.66 lakh crore evaluated, 256 sanctioned (Aug 2026)

why_it_matters.text: Gati Shakti builds nothing itself. It decides which projects get planned together: a road, a rail line, a terminal and a port that once came out of separate ministries are now laid over one map before approval. Its industrial effect comes through that sequencing.

The evidence trail now shows up in approvals. When the Cabinet approved the ₹20,667 crore Sarkhej–Dholera rail line to India’s first fab node in May 2026, the release said the project was planned on the PM-Gati Shakti National Master Plan.

That is why Techadyant treats Gati Shakti as the cross-cutting layer, not one programme among six. Bharatmala, Sagarmala, the freight corridors, the industrial corridors and ULIP all meet the industrial node through it.

timeline.label: Railways introduce the Gati Shakti Cargo Terminal policy

gaps.title: Evaluated is not built
gaps.detail: Of 396 projects evaluated through the NPG, 256 were sanctioned and 198 were under implementation (Aug 2026). The NPG count measures planning throughput, not delivered infrastructure.

gaps.title: Sequencing gaps persist at the node
gaps.detail: Even with NMP planning, Dholera gets road access first (the NE-8 expressway opened for testing in Feb 2026) and rail later (Sarkhej–Dholera completion up to 2030-31). Integrated planning has not removed the time lag between modes.

gaps.title: The platform is not public
gaps.detail: Techadyant cannot see the NMP’s data layers and does not replicate them. This page works from what is published: approvals that cite the NMP, NPG counts and policy documents.

consequences.headline: Industrial nodes are becoming planning objects, not just destinations

claims.text: The 2021 plan listed industrial corridors (11 corridors, 32 nodes), electronics manufacturing clusters, pharma clusters and defence corridors as layers alongside transport networks.
Once a cluster is a layer, its connectivity can be evaluated against it before approval. That favours nodes with a strategic anchor — the Dholera rail line is the clearest case in this Atlas.
118 Gati Shakti Cargo Terminals were commissioned by Jan 2026, with about ₹8,600 crore of private investment. The first terminal on private land along the Western DFC is at New Sanjali, Gujarat.
Terminals turn the rail backbone and the DFC into something a manufacturer can actually use. Where terminals sit relative to industrial nodes may matter more than corridor length.
A District Master Plan portal went to beta for 28 aspirational districts in Sep 2024, and the platform was extended to social-sector planning.
If districts plan on the same data frame as central ministries, smaller industrial locations become visible to project evaluators. This depends on the roll-out.

consequences.headline: A geospatial data market inside government

claims.text: The platform integrates 1,700+ data layers across 57 ministries and departments (Aug 2026).

Keeping layers current, validating them and connecting them to ULIP’s logistics APIs creates steady demand for GIS, data-engineering and analytics capability. Whether that is procured or built in-house is not documented.

consequences.headline: Fewer "road now, rail later" gaps — in principle

claims.text: Coordinated evaluation should shorten the periods when a new node has only one usable mode. The Dholera timeline shows that the gap is narrowed by planning but not closed by it.

supply_chain.text: Bulk inputs and components move by rail or road into the node.
Industrial corridors, electronics clusters and defence corridors are layers on the NMP.
Logistics and connectivity projects above ₹500 crore are evaluated by the NPG for network fit.
Gati Shakti Cargo Terminals link factories to rail: 118 commissioned.
Ports, shipping and airports are NMP sectors, so gateway projects are evaluated against the same map.
Lower friction across the chain may show up as lower delivered cost — the effect the platform is designed for, not one measured here.

related_programmes.note: The NPG had evaluated 115 NH/road projects (~13,500 km) by Mar 2025.
Ports, shipping and waterways are NMP sectors.
Railways are an NMP sector; the GCT policy puts terminals on the Western DFC.
PIB presents ULIP’s private-sector uptake (930+ companies) as part of the Gati Shakti logistics story.

include.reason: Covers the logistics system Gati Shakti plans.

data_gaps: The Aug 2026 NPG figures come from a secondary report of a PIB release that has not been independently retrieved.
The NMP’s layer inventory is not public; this page cannot say which industrial nodes are mapped.
Beyond the Sarkhej–Dholera rail line, which projects serving this Atlas’s industrial nodes passed the NPG is not documented.
Locations of the 118 commissioned cargo terminals are not yet mapped against industrial nodes.

programmes.name: Bharatmala Pariyojana
programmes.lead_ministry: Ministry of Road Transport & Highways (NHAI, NHIDCL)
programmes.question: Which industrial locations did the corridor network make more reachable — and which parts of the programme lagged behind?
programmes.stage_note: Phase-I awarding has closed: new sanctions were discontinued from November 2023. Awarded corridors are still being completed.

launch.label: Phase-I approved by the CCEA on 24 Oct 2017

time_horizon.text: Phase-I was originally targeted for 2021-22. No current completion date has been captured.

programmes.geography: National highway network — economic, inter-corridor, feeder, border and port-connectivity routes

glance.label: Phase-I scope
glance.value: 34,800 km, including ~10,000 km of residual NHDP

ledger.label: Cost of awarded length
ledger.value: ₹8,46,588 crore for 26,316 km — 158% of the 2017 estimate; MoRTH’s revised estimate ₹10.95 lakh crore

why_it_matters.text: Bharatmala matters less for the kilometres it adds than for how it chose them: by corridor, along origin–destination freight routes. Corridors change which industrial locations are cheap to reach, and so where new capacity is likely to go.

In practice it became an expressway programme. By March 2023, greenfield expressways were 302.75% awarded and 119.75% completed against their approved length, while coastal and port connectivity roads were 20.75% awarded and 5.2% completed.
The node-level effect is visible at Dholera: the 109 km NE-8 expressway, built under Bharatmala, cut Ahmedabad–Dholera travel from 2 h 15 min to 45 min when it opened for testing in Feb 2026.

timeline.label: Audit snapshot: 26,316 km awarded, 13,499 km completed; no MMLP developed
Public Accounts Committee reports on the CAG audit

gaps.title: Cost escalation
gaps.detail: The sanctioned cost of the awarded length was ₹32.17 crore/km against ₹15.37 crore/km approved — 158% of the 2017 estimate (Mar 2023).

gaps.title: Logistics parks not delivered
gaps.detail: None of the 35 planned multimodal logistics parks had been developed by March 2023.

gaps.title: Port access lagged
gaps.detail: Coastal & port connectivity roads were 5.2% complete in March 2023 — the weakest component.

gaps.title: What replaced Phase-I awarding
gaps.detail: New Phase-I sanctions have been discontinued since November 2023. The successor framework for new highway sanctions is not captured here.

claims.text: NE-8 cut Ahmedabad–Dholera travel time from 2 h 15 min to 45 min (Feb 2026).
For a greenfield node, the first fast road link is often what makes construction, workforce and early logistics practical before rail arrives.

consequences.headline: Trunk speed improved faster than the first and last mile

claims.text: Expressways over-delivered while MMLPs (0 of 35) and port-connectivity roads (5.2%) lagged as of Mar 2023.
Freight gains on the trunk can be absorbed at port gates and consolidation points that the programme did not build.

consequences.headline: Export gateways were the weak link

claims.text: Coastal & port connectivity was 20.75% awarded and 5.2% completed (Mar 2023).
The port leg is now addressed partly through Sagarmala’s port-connectivity pillar, so gateway access depends on two programmes.

The Bengaluru–Chennai Expressway, built under Bharatmala Phase-I, is described as a priority corridor of the Chennai–Bengaluru Industrial Corridor, with industrial areas and a proposed MMLP on its Karnataka section.
Where highway and industrial-corridor planning coincide, the highway becomes the corridor’s spine — the pattern to watch at other NICDP nodes.

consequences.headline: Road remains the default mode for time-sensitive inputs

claims.text: Faster corridors make road more competitive against rail for components and finished goods even as the DFC opens. That may slow the modal shift the freight corridors were built for.

supply_chain.text: Components and materials move by road over economic and feeder corridors.
Industrial nodes gain fast road access — e.g. Dholera via NE-8.
The 35 planned MMLPs had not been developed as of Mar 2023 — the missing consolidation layer.
Domestic markets gain most directly; export gains depend on the port leg.

related_programmes.note: 115 NH/road projects (~13,500 km) evaluated through the NPG by Mar 2025.
Both fund port connectivity: Bharatmala’s coastal & port roads and Sagarmala’s port-connectivity pillar.
MMLPs were planned under the Bharatmala umbrella; none developed by Mar 2023.

corridor_refs.note: The Bengaluru–Chennai Expressway (Bharatmala Phase-I) is described as a priority corridor of the CBIC.

include.reason: Covers road freight and logistics parks.

data_gaps: The May 2026 progress figures come from a press report of a Rajya Sabha reply; the primary text is not yet pinned.
Component-wise progress after March 2023 is not captured.
Expenditure is captured only to February 2025.
The successor framework for highway sanctions after Phase-I is not documented here.
Corridor alignments are not mapped; the footprint shows only projects linked to this Atlas’s nodes.

programmes.name: Sagarmala Programme
programmes.angle: Port-led development and India’s maritime industrial geography.
programmes.question: Is industry moving towards the ports, or are the ports only getting bigger?
programmes.stage_note: Projects are being completed under the five pillars. A Sagarmala 2.0 has been proposed but not approved.

time_horizon.text: Open-ended. Guided by Maritime India Vision 2030 and Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047; Sagarmala 2.0 proposed in 2026.

programmes.geography: Coastline, major and non-major ports, coastal States/UTs and national waterways

ledger.label: Completed
ledger.value: 315 projects · ₹1.57 lakh crore (~26% of portfolio value)

ledger.label: Sagarmala 2.0
ledger.value: Proposed: ₹85,482 crore budgetary support · ₹3.6 lakh crore total investment

why_it_matters.text: Sagarmala is less about ports than about where industry sits relative to them. Its distinctive pillar is port-led industrialisation: putting processing next to the gateway so that a land leg disappears from the supply chain.
By project count the programme is well advanced — 315 of 845 projects completed. By value it is not: completed projects account for ₹1.57 of ₹6.06 lakh crore, about a quarter (24 Mar 2026).
That gap suggests the large-ticket items — new ports and industrial zones — are the ones still to come. Those are the items that would change industrial geography.

components.progress: Perspective plans prepared for all 14 CEZs

gaps.title: Value lags count
gaps.detail: Completed projects are 37% of the portfolio by count but about 26% by value (24 Mar 2026).

gaps.title: CEZs are still plans
gaps.detail: The 14 Coastal Economic Zones are proposed with perspective plans; notification and land status are not documented here.

gaps.title: Pillar-wise progress
gaps.detail: The latest release gives no project or value split by pillar.

consequences.headline: Gateway throughput and speed are rising

claims.text: Major ports handled a record 915.17 MT in FY 2025-26, and average vessel turnaround fell to 49.5 hours in 2025 from 96 hours in 2014.
Faster turnaround lowers the cost of using an Indian gateway rather than transhipping. That matters most for container-heavy manufacturing exports.

consequences.headline: Hinterland links are funded port by port

claims.text: A ₹132.51 crore road over bridge at Deendayal Port’s LC-235 crossing was approved under Sagarmala to ease cargo evacuation (Apr 2026).
Deendayal is the gateway port this Atlas records for the Sanand semiconductor node. Port-gate works like this affect node logistics without ever naming the node.

consequences.headline: Port-led industrialisation is the unbuilt pillar

claims.text: 14 CEZs are proposed with perspective plans.
If CEZs move to notified land, import-heavy processing (energy, chemicals, metals) is the most likely early mover. None is documented as a CEZ unit here.

consequences.headline: River and coastal routes add a mode

claims.text: Inland-waterway cargo grew from 18.10 MT in FY 2013-14 to 145.5 MT in FY 2024-25.
For bulk inputs, a waterway leg can replace road. Its industrial relevance depends on whether terminals sit near clusters.
SDCL was restructured in June 2025 as a maritime-focused NBFC and sanctioned about ₹4,300 crore of loans by Dec 2025.
A dedicated lender changes who can finance port-linked projects, including private terminals and shipbuilding-adjacent industry.

supply_chain.text: Imported energy, feedstocks and components arrive through major and non-major ports.
Port-adjacent processing is planned through 14 proposed CEZs.
Port-connectivity projects link the port gate to road and rail.
Coastal and inland-waterway terminals add a non-road leg (145.5 MT IWT cargo, FY25).
Major ports: 915.17 MT in FY 2025-26; turnaround 49.5 h (2025).
Export markets — the leg where turnaround and port charges set competitiveness.

related_programmes.note: Ports, shipping and waterways are NMP sectors.
Coastal shipping and inland waterways transport is one of Sagarmala’s five pillars.
Major-port throughput is the outcome measure Sagarmala reports.

data_gaps: Pillar-wise project counts and values are not captured.
CEZ notification, land and anchor-unit status are not documented.
Port coordinates for Mumbai and JNPA are not yet in the infrastructure registry.
Which Sagarmala projects serve this Atlas’s industrial nodes is documented only for Deendayal Port.
